knowledge_type_note: Terminology for a specific prophylactic move and the square it creates.

history.notes: A German loanword in English chess writing; no coinage researched.

engine_era_note: Engines make luft when it is needed and not otherwise, and are unimpressed by it as a routine move. That matches the conditional reading rather than the habitual one.

preconditions: A castled king with its shield pawns unmoved
A pawn move that creates a flight square
indicators_for: Heavy pieces remain, so back-rank mates are live
The opponent cannot storm the king's wing
The back rank is already defended by only one piece
indicators_against: The opponent has castled on the other wing and can throw pawns forward
The advanced pawn becomes a hook for a specific break
The tempo is needed elsewhere in a sharp position
false_positive_traps: Making luft is not automatically prudent. The same move is a hook against an opponent who can storm, and this is the standard error.
Luft is unnecessary when the back rank is adequately defended or when no heavy pieces remain.

typical_plans: Make luft in a quiet moment, before it is forced
Prefer the pawn move that creates the fewest weaknesses
typical_moves: g3 / ...g6 — more committal, since it weakens two squares
typical_pawn_structures: f2-g2-h2 intact, with h3 the usual choice
strategic_consequences: Permanently uncovers the squares the pawn left

exceptions: Against a queenside-castled opponent, luft is a hook and usually a concession.
With no heavy pieces left, back-rank mate is not a threat and luft is a wasted move.
limitations: Trivially detectable; whether it is wise is entirely conditional on the opponent's attacking prospects.
misconceptions: That making luft is always sensible prophylaxis. It is conditional, and the condition is whether the opponent can attack that wing.

by_level.beginner: Move one pawn in front of your castled king so the king has somewhere to go if it gets checked on the back row.
by_level.intermediate: Luft. Worth playing when heavy pieces are on and back-rank mates are live — but it also weakens squares permanently, so check they cannot storm that wing.
by_level.advanced: A conditional move. The same h3 is useful prophylaxis in a quiet position and a hook against a queenside-castled opponent.
by_level.master: Measured: in a controlled test one tempo of luft turned a mate in one into a mate in thirty. The cost is the hook, and which dominates is the whole question.

by_depth.short: A pawn move giving the king an escape square.
by_depth.normal: Luft — German for air. Advancing a pawn in front of the castled king gives it a flight square and removes back-rank mates, at the cost of permanently weakening the squares the pawn left.
by_depth.deep: A castled king behind three unmoved pawns has no escape square, which is what makes back-rank mates work. One pawn move fixes it — and in a controlled test in this base, moving a pawn from h7 to h6 turned a mate in one into a mate in thirty. The cost is that the vacated squares are uncovered for good and the advanced pawn becomes a hook the opponent can attack to open a file. So the same move is good or bad on one question: can they realistically storm this wing? In a quiet position it is free; against an opponent castled the other way it is a concession.

explanations.lesson: Make luft when heavy pieces are on and nobody can storm you. Against an opponent castled the other way, that same pawn move is a target.

definition_short: German for 'air': a pawn move in front of the castled king that gives it an escape square and removes back-rank mates.
definition_long:
A castled king behind three unmoved pawns has no escape square, which is what makes back-rank mates possible. Advancing one of them — usually the h-pawn to h3 or h6 — creates a flight square and eliminates the whole family of back-rank tactics at a stroke.

The cost is exactly the cost of any shield-pawn move: the squares the pawn has left are permanently uncovered, and the advanced pawn itself becomes a HOOK the opponent can attack to force a file open.

So the same move is good or bad depending on one question: can the opponent realistically storm your king? In a quiet position, or with queens off, h3 is a free and useful move. Against an opponent castled on the other wing with mobile pawns, the identical move hands them something to bite on with ...g5-g4.

Its value is measurable and large. In a controlled test in this knowledge base, moving one pawn from h7 to h6 turned a mate in one into a mate in thirty.
